pr_title: Add support for double-width/double-height lines in conhost
pr_body:
This PR adds support for the VT line rendition attributes, which allow
for double-width and double-height line renditions. These renditions are
enabled with the `DECDWL` (double-width line) and `DECDHL`
(double-height line) escape sequences. Both reset to the default
rendition with the `DECSWL` (single-width line) escape sequence. For now
this functionality is only supported by the GDI renderer in conhost.

There are a lot of changes, so this is just a general overview of the
main areas affected.

Previously it was safe to assume that the screen had a fixed width, at
least for a given point in time. But now we need to deal with the
possibility of different lines have different widths, so all the
functions that are constrained by the right border (text wrapping,
cursor movement operations, and sequences like `EL` and `ICH`) now need
to lookup the width of the active line in order to behave correctly.

Similarly it used to be safe to assume that buffer and screen
coordinates were the same thing, but that is no longer true. Lots of
places now need to translate back and forth between coordinate systems
dependent on the line rendition. This includes clipboard handling, the
conhost color selection and search, accessibility location tracking and
screen reading, IME editor positioning, "snapping" the viewport, and of
course all the rendering calculations.

For the rendering itself, I've had to introduce a new
`PrepareLineTransform` method that the render engines can use to setup
the necessary transform matrix for a given line rendition. This is also
now used to handle the horizontal viewport offset, since that could no
longer be achieved just by changing the target coordinates (on a double
width line, the viewport offset may be halfway through a character).

I've also had to change the renderer's existing `InvalidateCursor`
method to take a `SMALL_RECT` rather than a `COORD`, to allow for the
cursor being a variable width. Technically this was already a problem,
because the cursor could occupy two screen cells when over a
double-width character, but now it can be anything between one and four
screen cells (e.g. a double-width character on the double-width line).

In terms of architectural changes, there is now a new `lineRendition`
field in the `ROW` class that keeps track of the line rendition for each
row, and several new methods in the `ROW` and `TextBuffer` classes for
manipulating that state. This includes a few helper methods for handling
the various issues discussed above, e.g. position clamping and
translating between coordinate systems.

## Validation Steps Performed

I've manually confirmed all the double-width and double-height tests in
_Vttest_ are now working as expected, and the _VT100 Torture Test_ now
renders correctly (at least the line rendition aspects). I've also got
my own test scripts that check many of the line rendition boundary cases
and have confirmed that those are now passing.

I've manually tested as many areas of the conhost UI that I could think
of, that might be affected by line rendition, including things like
searching, selection, copying, and color highlighting. For
accessibility, I've confirmed that the _Magnifier_ and _Narrator_
correctly handle double-width lines. And I've also tested the Japanese
IME, which while not perfect, is at least useable.

Closes #7865

This is the only thing I noticed in writing `big.txt` between `main` and this branch. Note that big.txt doesn't output anything but standard text in standard lines.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/18221333/104778881-f24c4c80-5732-11eb-9341-ee37908ef606.png)

It looks like we're calling `Set/ModifyWorldTransform` to GDI even when there isn't really anything to talk about. Unfortunately when I expand it, it looks like this goes all the way into kernel to resolve that there's nothing to change. So if we could not call it when there's nothing to be done on our side, it would probably save us something.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/18221333/104779054-422b1380-5733-11eb-8373-628eb116c0ad.png)

It does look like its a very small amount in CPU time, but there's probably some amount of thunk/kernel switching that isn't being accounted for here too that we could avoid.

> It looks like we're calling `Set/ModifyWorldTransform` to GDI even when there isn't really anything to talk about.

I'm really glad you spotted that. I actually had checks in place to avoid setting and resetting the transform unnecessarily in the `PrepareLineTransform` and `ResetLineTransform` methods, but I got caught out by the fact that -0.0 and 0.0 aren't equal.

And I just realised there's also the special case handling for the inverted cursor, which has to "uninvert" itself when scrolling, and that requires setting a transform first. So that's also going to need a check to avoid the transform when it's just the identity matrix.

OK. I've added the requested comments, made the `GetTextRects` parameters explicit, and improved the checks to avoid unnecessary transform changes. You shouldn't be seeing any `Set/ModifyWorldTransform` calls now if you're just rendering regular single-width text, with no horizontal viewport offset.

issue_context.title: Add support for double width/height lines
issue_context.body:
# Description of the new feature/enhancement

The VT100 (and later DEC terminals) had a bunch of operations that could alter the width and height of characters on a per-line basis: [`DECDWL`](https://vt100.net/docs/vt510-rm/DECDWL.html), [`DECDHL`](https://vt100.net/docs/vt510-rm/DECDHL.html), and [`DECSWL`](https://vt100.net/docs/vt510-rm/DECSWL.html). Despite their limitations, they're still quite useful for sprucing up a UI.

As an example, here's a UI for a chess app rendered with and without line attribute support:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4181424/95500478-c0428600-099e-11eb-991f-2ca9cdf47fce.png)

# Proposed technical implementation details (optional)

I've been playing around with a POC of this for a while now, and I've come to realise there's actually a lot more work involved than you might first expect. Other than the basic rendering of characters, we need to handle text decoration, cursor rendering, selection marking, window resizing, mouse position detection, and every VT operation that depends on window boundaries will potentially need to take line attributes into account.

So before I spend more time on this, I wanted to make sure it's something you'd be happy to accept. I should say that I'm inclined to make it conhost-only to start with. I have also looked at the WT side of things, but that basically doubles the workload, and there are extra complications introduced by conpty that I don't have a good answer for.
comments:
I'm sure we'd be happy to accept, but I think the real trick here is going to be the conpty bit. I really have no idea how the renderer could be updated to support such a thing.

I guess if we start by scoping this to conhost only, then it's not like it's going to be any worse in the Terminal than it currently is. I'd probably break it into 3 PRs - one for conhost, one for rendering with conpty, and a final one for implementing in Terminal.
If there's a way for conpty to support this, then my working Sixel implementation might also benefit from it.

My plan for this is to leave it conhost-only until we are in a position to rethink the conpty architecture. I would have advised the same thing for Sixel, but I thought maybe you already had a solution for that.

review_comments:
This is a lot of creativity for multiplying and dividing by 2. 

I don't mind the pre-optimization (though I'm pretty sure the optimizer in the linker or in the processor microcode would catch this one and do it for you), but could you at least leave the comment of what this is in less obtuse math?

```
// Use shift right to quickly divide left/right by 2 for double width lines.
```
Also thanks for starting me off with a thinker on this PR. So much for easing into it! :P
OK I guess you had to use this EVERYWHERE so that's why the pre-optimization.

Yeah, there's probably an element of premature optimization here. I was less concerned about speed though - I honestly wouldn't know if an imul or idiv is significantly worse than a shift on a modern processor. But I was horrified by the amount of code I was introducing in my initial implementation, and the shifts were definitely an improvement in that respect.

The current version is actually a bit of a compromise - the optimizer doesn't handle inlining of these functions very well - but I was also trying to keep some of the messy details hidden in the helper functions, and not bloat the rest of the source too much.

There was also another reason I preferred the shifts - at least for division. If the values are negative, then a div doesn't round in the right direction, whereas a shift does. I don't _think_ we need to support negative numbers in the current usage, but it felt safer knowing that these functions would do the right thing if that ever did occur.

I agree this could definitely do with some commenting though.
All I have to say here is "I am so flippin' glad it is PER ROW and not randomly sprayable throughout the whole thing PER CELL." Can you imagine that nightmare?
Just the quick note over here too about fast multiply/divide for these to reduce reader brain stress.
I wish this was all til::rectangle but I understand why it'd be weird to convert this one vertical when the rest are still all using the non-til types.
Yeah, I did go through a few different options here, but it just made everything so much easier to stick with the `SMALL_RECT` that was being used everywhere else.
Thanks for not missing `WddmConEngine` and `BgfxEngine`.

Confirm for me...

Presumably if you have a double height row, shrink the window, it'll run through reflow and now you'll have... 2 rows that are double height. Right?

And then if you grow the window wider again, it'll run through here and manage to find space in the single row again and we'll lose the second double height row because the `newBufferPos.X` won't be 0 when it tries to fill up the regrown space right of the original line. And the fact that there's a lot of `.Right` space on the spill over row will cause us to just jump down after collapsing it back together and the 2nd one will disappear. Right?

> Presumably if you have a double height row, shrink the window, it'll run through reflow and now you'll have... 2 rows that are double height. Right?

No. A double height row is basically two lines with identical text - one rendering the double height top, and the other rendering the bottom. Once the top portion wraps, it's just going to split the double height rendition in half with a normal size line in between. No matter what line attribute you assign to the wrapped portion, it's not going to make much sense, so I don't even try to do anything fancy. But if you regrow the window and it unwraps again, it should at least go back to normal.

I kind of went with a minimalist solution here. Basically it should work reasonably for the simple cases, but once the content wraps, I don't think there are any good solutions - these attributes were just never expected to be used that way.
Ah that's fine. Okay. Thanks for clarifying.
Huh, we fill *after* we reset the rendition? I don't totally understand why, but I trust your homework here.
erm we fill *before*.

I don't think it matters. The fill operation doesn't care about line renditions, so I suspect it would work in either order. I do know that this sequence works correctly as is - it's one of my manual test cases.
I've just double checked this and the order doesn't make any difference. In both case the lines are reset to single width and the screen is completely filled with Es.

Why reset the line rendition separately here instead of inside of `DoSrvPrivateFillRegion` or even further down like in every consumer of `screenInfo.Write`/`TextBuffer::WriteLine` much like how line wraps are added/removed/left alone in certain common cases like rectangular fills?

I did consider doing something like that, but not all rectangular fills are meant to reset the line rendition. For example you could clear a double-width line with `EL` or `ECH`, and that would result in the full width being filled, but shouldn't reset the rendition.
Fair enough.

This is for when a LF moves you into a non-single-width line, right?

Assuming there's no deferred EOL breakage we're concerned with here since this _is_ a cursor movement.
Correct. The delayed EOL flag is going to be reset as soon as we set the cursor position, so I don't think this should break anything in that regard.

Oh my god what. This is a thing?! You're telling me I could have done High DPI with a transform?!

Does it impact the fidelity of the scaled text at all (is extra aliasing visible) or does it work perfectly as if you had set the font size larger?

(Also, I'm a little worried that we should only do this and only set the transform if we need it because it might cause all sorts of GDI stuff to take a different codepath that is slower in the common case. My hope is that it's intelligent enough to not have a detriment if you have advanced mode on with an identity transform. But... we'll have to watch out for this.)

> Does it impact the fidelity of the scaled text at all (is extra aliasing visible) or does it work perfectly as if you had set the font size larger?

It looks pretty smooth to me. It's definitely not just pixel-doubling. However, I should mention that I've noticed block characters not always lining up perfectly when double sized, but I'm not sure that's necessarily the fault of the transforms, and I didn't think it was worth worrying about too much until someone complained.

> it might cause all sorts of GDI stuff to take a different codepath that is slower in the common case

Yeah, I did wonder about that too. I'm not sure you can just turn it on and off as you need it though. And note that the renderer is now using transforms for the viewport offset too, so it's not just the double-size renditions that need it. But if it it's a significant problem, I can try and see what it would take to enable it on demand - I suspect it would be messy though.
Nah based on the wpr... It didn't have a big impact just for setting the mode. So ignore this one.
Are you sure about that? There's a provision in the `conhost.exe` to set your cursor height to 100%. Which I would think would go double height on a double height line.

As explained above, a double height line is actually two lines with identical content. So the cursor could be on either the top half or the bottom half of that line, and would only cover the height of the portion that it's on. Technically both halves may not even be there - you could quite easily have the bottom half of a double height line with a single height line above it.

That said, I don't know for a fact that the original hardware terminals worked that way. It just seemed the most reasonable approach to take, and I haven't come across any terminal emulators that do things differently.
Alright.
Double height here counts as double width?
Oh, I didn't realize that double-height lines _were_ by necessity double-width.

This is thanks to you adding a `false` (for useBufferCoordinates) to the text rect computation in Selection, right?

I couldn't immediately evaluate this as true, but I did look at consumers in Selection of the endpoints that are populated through this function and trust it well enough.

The only place `GetWordBoundary` is called is from the window mouse event handler. It is passed the mouse position in screen coordinates, and then expects to receive the calculated word boundary in the same coordinate system. See here:
https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/blob/b1e1c7cdf4efa1ca4e0a495f6b90fd83ca8b5633/src/interactivity/win32/windowio.cpp#L803-L806

Right -- and that's fed into Selection, which (as far as I can tell) only uses it for updating the renderer's invalidation range. I couldn't determine if anyone was using the stuff in Selection in buffer coords. :smile:

It is a bit confusing. Different parts of the `Selection` class use different coordinate systems. For example the `ColorSelection` methods expect buffer coordinates, and the `GetSelectionRects` method returns buffer coordinates, but the internal anchor positions are stored in screen coordinates. This was a bit of a nightmare to sort out, and although I tried my best to catch as many of these cases as I could, it wouldn't be a huge surprise to me if there were others that I missed.
